extracted.intended_audience: regulatory economists, OSHA analysts, stakeholders (employers, worker representatives), and public commenters on the OSHA heat NPRM
extracted.subtask_description: Methods, inclusion criteria, assumptions, and calculations OSHA uses to estimate labor productivity losses from heat, translate those losses into equivalent minutes per 8-hour shift, and estimate employer cost savings from if‑needed and scheduled rest breaks under the proposed heat standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisions requiring training upon hire and annually
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring training on occupational heat-related risks and protections covered by this standard (e.g., rest breaks, water) to employees upon hire and each year can enhance knowledge of heat safe work practices, reducing risk of HRIs among less experienced or vulnerable workers;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA states this as a provision of the proposed standard intended to reinforce protections; training frequency is upon hire and annually and is tied to reducing HRIs among vulnerable workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training in language and literacy-appropriate format with Q&A
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring the provision of training in a language and literacy level appropriate for staff along with the opportunities for questions and answers ensures heat protections (e.g., paid rest breaks, cool drinking water) are understood and accessible to all;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance emphasizes cultural and linguistic accessibility of training so protections are comprehensible and usable by workers who may face language/literacy barriers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acclimatization protocol plus paid rest breaks and other supports
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring an acclimatization protocol along with paid rest breaks that include adequate drinking water, shade (or air conditioning), and medical attention (if necessary) at initial and high heat triggers foster non-exploitive treatment of non-salaried vulnerable workers (e.g., farmworkers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed standard ties acclimatization and specified support elements (water, shade/AC, medical attention) to trigger points (initial and high heat), and frames these as protections for vulnerable non-salaried workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee measures to avoid overheating (three measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: When working in hot conditions, OSHA assumes that employees can take three different measures to avoid overheating: (1) pace themselves; (2) take rest breaks if needed; (3) take scheduled rest breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three measures are not mutually exclusive and are used to classify worker behavior in studies and to model changes in productivity when rest-break policies change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group definitions based on allowed measures (Groups 1–3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Group #1: employees who only use pacing (no rest breaks). Group #2: employees who take rest breaks if needed and pace. Group #3: employees who take scheduled rest breaks, may take rest breaks if needed, and pace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA uses these groupings to map study conditions to real-world workplace rest-break policies, and to estimate how productivity losses differ under each policy scenario.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study inclusion criteria for primary approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Included studies generally must: measure labor productivity over a range of temperatures so comparisons can be made between a cool (REF) condition and HOT condition(s); provide enough information on weather conditions so HI could be estimated; collect labor productivity data; report productivity as output per worker, per hour, or per day; and provide information as to whether breaks were offered and, if so, how long and frequent the breaks were.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA searched literature and considered only studies meeting these criteria; studies failing these were excluded (detailed exclusion reasons in table VIII.H.A.3.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Information to extract from each included study
rubrics_metrics.description: Each included study was evaluated for: (1) which measure(s) employees took to avoid overheating (Measures #1–#3) to assign to Groups #1–#3; (2) weather data describing the REF (cool) condition so HI can be calculated; (3) weather data describing the HOT condition(s) so HI can be calculated; and (4) labor productivity at both REF and HOT conditions to compute loss (%) and rate of loss per 1 °F HI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA converts each study's REF and HOT conditions to HI (using ambient/dry bulb temp and RH) and computes productivity loss per 1 °F HI to enable comparability across heterogeneous studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate productivity loss to rate per 1 °F heat index
rubrics_metrics.description: After calculating the rate of labor productivity loss per 1 °F HI, OSHA calculated the cumulative labor productivity loss as a percentage relative to the REF condition at the initial heat trigger (HI of 80 °F) and high heat trigger (HI of 90 °F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standardizes heterogeneous study results by expressing changes in productivity as percent loss per °F HI and then computing losses at standard trigger HI values for comparison and aggregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 8-hour (480 minute) work shift to convert percent loss to minutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Labor productivity loss was then translated into equivalent minutes of lost work time by multiplying by an 8-hour work shift (480 minutes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA consistently uses 480 minutes as the baseline shift length when reporting minutes lost per shift due to pacing/productivity loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume productivity at or below REF condition equals 100%
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless otherwise specified, productivity at or below the REF condition is 100%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This baseline assumption is used to calculate percent losses relative to the REF condition; changing the REF would change the measured loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume linear relationship between HI and productivity loss above REF
rubrics_metrics.description: Above the REF condition, the relationship between HI and labor productivity loss is linear, i.e., the rate of loss (per 1 °F HI) is a constant. Therefore, the productivity loss function for any firm can be fully characterized by two parameters: the REF condition and the rate of loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA applies a constant percent-per-°F loss derived from study data to interpolate/extrapolate losses at the initial and high heat triggers; this is an explicit modeling assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumed break durations for Groups 2 and 3
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees in Group 2 are allowed to take up to 10 minutes of rest breaks if needed (with 2–4 minutes of travel time to/from break areas). Employees in Group 3 are allowed to take 30 minutes of scheduled rest breaks, along with 5 minutes of rest breaks if needed (with 2–4 minutes of travel time to/from break areas for each break).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These assumed break durations define the empirical comparators for estimating how much pacing remains under different break policies and underpin the mapping from study conditions to Group categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume productivity gains from new/scheduled breaks equal study-measured differences
rubrics_metrics.description: An employee's expected productivity gains from taking new or newly scheduled rest breaks (versus not taking breaks or taking only if‑needed breaks) can be estimated by differences in productivity losses due to pacing, as measured at the initial temperature (i.e., trigger) at which the rest break policy goes into effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA uses between-group differences observed in studies to infer the productivity improvement from policy changes; this assumes the studies capture the causal effect of breaks on pacing/productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust productivity-loss rates when study break schedules differ from proposed rule
rubrics_metrics.description: When a study's break schedule differs from the proposed rule (e.g., study sugarcane cutters given 60 minutes total vs proposed 35 minutes), OSHA adjusts the measured rate of productivity loss by the ratio of percentages of the work shift spent in breaks for the two scenarios (e.g., multiplied by 1.52).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA explicitly scales study-derived productivity-loss rates to account for different amounts of time spent on breaks so the rates reflect the proposed rule's break schedule; the example given multiplies by the ratio of break-time proportions.
